stem:
Joseph is a 13-month-old boy brought to the emergency department after his mother found him choking and gagging in the kitchen next to a container of spilled nuts. He is alert, has audible stridor and subcostal retractions, is intermittently coughing, and has normal colour. His vital signs are RR 66/min, HR 160/min, BP 88/56, Temp 37.1°C, and SaO2 93% on blow-by oxygen.

Which one of the following is your first step in management?

options.text: Obtain IV access and prefer for intubation and ventilation

explanation: This is a suspected foreign body airway obstruction in a child with partial obstruction who is still coughing and maintaining colour. The first step is age-appropriate choking first aid. In a 13-month-old, back blows are the first intervention; abdominal thrusts are used in older children/adults, and no blind airway manoeuvres or nebulised adrenaline are indicated.

citations.title: Practice Quiz: Emergency Medicine - Breathing difficulties

rationale: The key clinical clue is choking with a possible foreign body and partial airway obstruction in a child under 1–2 years old. Management starts with back blows (and chest thrusts if needed), not asthma/croup treatments or advanced airway management.

optionExplanations.A: Abdominal thrusts (Heimlich manoeuvre) are not the first-line manoeuvre in an infant/toddler this young.
optionExplanations.B: Nebulised adrenaline is for upper airway oedema such as croup, not choking from a foreign body.
optionExplanations.C: IV access and intubation are not the initial step in a child who is still breathing and coughing with suspected choking.
optionExplanations.D: He needs immediate age-appropriate first aid because he has signs of partial airway obstruction.
optionExplanations.E: Correct: for a 13-month-old with suspected choking and partial obstruction, start with back blows.
